content: 1. Syringes for all injections must meet specific implementation requirements. Existing documents will either be incorporated into or updated as part of the dissemination strategy, depending on their relevance. 2. The guideline is expected to be launched by the Director-General of WHO during a high-level meeting. Key stakeholders, including WHO partners, UN organizations, WHO regional offices, NGOs, and umbrella organizations of injection device manufacturers, will be invited to promote widespread adoption of the new policy guidance. 3. Despite limited studies, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), documenting the impact of safety-engineered syringes on syringe reuse and needlestick injuries (NSIs), WHO recommends that all countries transition by 2020 to the exclusive use of WHO-prequalified (or equivalent) safety-engineered injection devices. This includes reuse prevention (RUP) syringes and sharps injury protection (SIP) devices for therapeutic injections, except in cases where RUP features are unsuitable for specific medical procedures (e.g., intravenous line maintenance, local anesthesia, or nasal feeding). 4. National policies should be developed to ensure a smooth transition to safety-engineered devices. These policies should be based on national epidemiological data regarding syringe reuse rates and the frequency of NSIs among healthcare workers (HCWs). 5. WHO assessments over the past decade have shown that safety precautions are often not followed, exposing patients and HCWs to significant risks of bloodborne infections and injuries. This highlights the urgent need for improved injection safety practices. 6. Countries with a high burden of bloodborne diseases, high rates of syringe reuse, and high injection usage can request WHO assistance in gathering local epidemiological data to inform policy development. 7. Implementation of the guideline should consider available resources, existing injection safety and infection control policies, delivery platforms, current injection device suppliers, communication channels, and potential country stakeholders. 8. WHO will promote partnerships at the country level between policymakers, professional organizations, researchers, and civil society to facilitate policy development and implementation using the best available local evidence. 9. The introduction of RUP and SIP devices should be part of comprehensive injection safety plans. Education and communication efforts should target both patients and HCWs to raise awareness of the risks associated with unsafe injections and their potential to transmit bloodborne infections. 10. Appropriate training must be provided to healthcare providers on the use of selected safety devices before their formal introduction. Both rural and urban healthcare facilities, whether public or private, should be equipped with RUP and SIP devices. 11. Training programs should include existing quantification tools and procurement specifications to ensure proper implementation. 12. During the planning phase, sharps waste management and the potential environmental impact of new devices must be considered. Healthcare facilities should be supplied with adequate quantities of safety boxes for the safe collection of used devices, following the bundling principle. 13. RUP syringes are categorized into two types: Type 1, which operates automatically during or upon completion of a single use, and Type 2, which requires manual activation after a single use. In high-risk countries with prevalent syringe reuse, Type 1 RUP syringes are recommended to prevent infection and cross-contamination. 14. Post-marketing surveillance is necessary to monitor defects, effectiveness, and any issues encountered during the use of new safety devices. 15. A monitoring and evaluation plan with appropriate indicators should be established at all levels to assess the adoption, adaptation, and implementation of the guideline globally. Monitoring should also occur at the health service level. 16. Injection safety assessments, clinical audits, supervision, NSI surveillance, and reporting systems are essential tools for monitoring the implementation and impact of the policy recommendations. 17. Clearly defined indicators, aligned with locally agreed targets, are needed to measure progress. The uptake of safety-engineered syringes for all injections should serve as a process indicator for monitoring injection practices and preventing bloodborne virus transmission in healthcare settings. 18. The guideline will be reviewed as soon as new evidence becomes available, given the scarcity of studies on the impact of safety-engineered syringes on NSIs and syringe reuse, as well as the cost-effectiveness of such devices. 19. A guideline review group will be convened to evaluate new evidence and revise recommendations if necessary. The Department of Service Delivery and Safety, along with internal WHO partners, will coordinate the guideline update following formal WHO procedures. 20. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to evaluate the guideline during its review process.
